newsitem.title: USA: FAA exploring possible problems in 727 freighters.
newsitem.headline: FAA exploring possible problems in 727 freighters.

text.p: Federal Aviation Administration officials are investigating potential structural problems with converted Boeing Co. 727 freighters used throughout the air cargo industry, an agency spokesman said Tuesday.
Spokesman Mitch Barker said recent inspections had uncovered "possible discrepancies in the designs and installation practices" used in some of the conversions, which had been done with FAA approval.

He said the problem did not affect 727s that were originally delivered by Boeing as freighters but said the FAA was looking into passenger aircraft converted under engineering designs approved by the agency.

News of the FAA inquiry, which has been going on for several months, has roiled stocks of some air cargo stocks this week because of concern the agency will limit payloads while the structural problems are fixed.

A spokesman for Federal Express Corp., which operates 163 Boeing 727s including 120 that were converted into freighters out of a fleet of 564 planes, said the carrier was confident in the engineering and design work it did to convert the Boeing trijets.
"We are very confident that our aircraft are structurally sound and airworthy," said the spokesman, Greg Rossiter. "We feel there's no financial or operational risk."

Tom Christopher, chairman and chief executive officer of Kitty Hawk Inc., a cargo carrier that operates 12 Boeing 727s out of a fleet of 26 aircraft, said he expected the problem to be resolved quickly and cheaply.
Christopher said the FAA likely would issue a bulletin in the first quarter of 1997 ordering carriers to strengthen the plane's floor and the bulkhead that separates cargo from the cockpit.
"We anticipate we will have six months to a year to make the minor modification to the airplane," he said.

Scott Hamilton, editor of the trade magazine Commercial Aviation Report, said the FAA might "economically ground" the airplanes by limiting cargo loads on the affected planes to 3,000 pounds per pallet from as much as 10,000 pounds until the modifications are made.

But an executive for Burlington Air Express Inc., which operates 11 converted 727s out of 31 airplanes, said even such a limit would allow the jets to carry 44,000 pounds of cargo, which he said was not too far below average.
Barker said the FAA had no plans to act until discussions are held with owners and operators of the aircraft, which he estimated would begin in late January.
